Shared Variance and Relative Importance

How much does each predictor really explain, and does the answer depend on how we ask?

Author

Supplementary note

Published

September 4, 2026

1 Why this note exists

The paper’s stepwise table (Model 1 to Model 5) reports coefficients and t-values for each predictor. It is tempting to read those t-values as a ranking of importance, and an earlier draft of section 4.2 did exactly that. That reading is not safe, for a reason worth setting out carefully.

In a multiple regression, each coefficient describes a predictor’s unique contribution: the association that remains once every other predictor is held constant. Where predictors are uncorrelated, unique contribution and total contribution are the same thing and nothing is lost. Where predictors are correlated, a large part of the variance they explain is shared between them, and the model has no way to attribute that shared part to one variable rather than another. It simply goes unallocated. A variable that overlaps heavily with the others will therefore show a modest t-value even when it accounts for a great deal of the outcome on its own.

Our three main predictors overlap a good deal, so this is not a hypothetical concern. This note quantifies it: it reports what each predictor explains on its own, what every combination of predictors explains, and how the shared variance is apportioned when we use a method designed for that purpose. It then asks the question that actually matters — whether the paper’s conclusions depend on which measure we choose.

The analysis sample is 12,208 school-years, the same rows used for the paper’s models, restricted to complete cases so that every model below is fitted on identical data.

2 How much do the predictors overlap?

Schools with more disadvantaged intakes have markedly lower prior attainment, and schools with higher absence also have lower prior attainment. These are not nuisance correlations to be controlled away; they are the structure of the problem. But they do mean that a large share of the variance in attainment is explained by these variables jointly, and any claim about which one matters most has to say how the joint part is being handled.

3 What each predictor explains on its own

The simplest question: fit each predictor alone against attainment, and record the \(R^2\). This is the total association, including everything the variable shares with the others.

On this measure prior attainment leads, absence follows, and disadvantage is third. Note how different this is from the t-values in the paper’s Model 3, where absence appears strongest and disadvantage weakest by a wide margin. The gap between the two pictures is precisely the shared variance.

4 Every combination of the three main predictors

The table below fits all eight possible subsets of disadvantage, absence and prior attainment, and reports both the model \(R^2\) and how each coefficient and t-value moves as its companions are added.

This is the shared-variance problem made visible. Disadvantage on its own carries a coefficient of about −0.20; with absence and prior attainment alongside it, that falls to roughly −0.05. Nothing about the schools has changed — only what else the model is being told.

Which of those numbers is “the effect of disadvantage” depends entirely on the question. If you want the total association between a school’s intake composition and its results, the first is closer. If you want the association that remains between two schools with the same absence and the same prior attainment, the last is closer. The paper needs the second, because its question is what happens if you change intake composition while everything else stays as it is — but it should not then describe that number as the importance of disadvantage in general, and section 3.2 now says so explicitly.

5 Apportioning the shared variance

Neither “\(R^2\) alone” nor “the coefficient in the full model” is a complete answer. The first hands each variable all of the shared variance; the second hands it none. The standard resolution is to average over every possible order in which the variables could enter: a variable’s contribution is computed when it enters first, second and third, and these are averaged. This is the Shapley value from cooperative game theory, known in this context as the LMG decomposition after Lindeman et al. (1980), and implemented for R by Grömping (2007).

The ranking of the top two does depend on the measure. By t-value, absence leads; by explanatory power alone and by the Shapley decomposition, prior attainment leads. This is exactly why the paper no longer rests any claim on the t-value ordering.

What does not change is the position of disadvantage: last under all three measures, whether it is credited with all of the shared variance, none of it, or an even split. The paper’s substantive argument depends only on that, and it is robust to the choice.

6 All nine predictors

The same decomposition across the full fixed-effect specification. With nine predictors there are \(2^9 = 512\) subsets and \(9! = 362{,}880\) orderings, so the Shapley values are computed from the subset lattice rather than by enumerating permutations — the two are mathematically identical, but the first is tractable.

The sum of the Shapley values is 0.709, which by construction equals the \(R^2\) of the full nine-predictor model — the decomposition allocates all of the explained variance and none of it twice.

7 What this means for the paper

Three conclusions, in order of how much they matter.

The importance ranking of the top two predictors is method-dependent, and the paper should not assert one. Section 4.2 previously ranked the three by t-value and called absence the most important. That has been rewritten: it now reports the t-values as measures of precision, states plainly that they cannot rank importance where predictors are correlated, and gives the explanatory-power and Shapley figures alongside. Section 4.3, which uses standardised coefficients from the full model, already placed prior attainment first; the two sections no longer contradict one another.

The paper’s argument does not depend on the choice. Concentrations of disadvantage rank last on every measure tried here. The claim the paper actually makes — that disadvantage concentration is a weak lever relative to absence, and that an admissions policy built on it is unlikely to deliver the gains sought — is unaffected by how the shared variance is apportioned.

Prior attainment is large but is not a lever. The measures above rank explanatory power, not actionability. Prior attainment is the single largest source of variation on two of the three measures, but it is fixed for any cohort already in secondary school: it describes the intake a school receives, not something the school or its authority can change. Once it is set aside as intake rather than lever, absence is the largest factor remaining that is open to intervention — which is the distinction section 4.3 draws and the one on which the policy argument rests.

8 A caveat on all of this

Every measure here is descriptive. None of them licenses a causal reading, and the relative-importance literature is explicit that these decompositions apportion variance explained, not effect (Grömping 2007). Two predictors can share variance because one causes the other, because a third thing causes both, or because they are alternative measurements of the same underlying disadvantage — and no decomposition of an observational dataset can tell these apart. That prior attainment, absence and disadvantage overlap so heavily is itself the substantive finding: they are facets of a single structure, and the policy question is not which is “most important” but which of them can actually be moved.

References

Grömping, Ulrike. 2007. “Relative Importance for Linear Regression in R: The Package relaimpo.” Journal of Statistical Software 17 (1): 1–27. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v017.i01.
